blocks.text: Do not log entire payloads by default. Large or secret-bearing requests can exhaust storage and expose sensitive data. Bound field lengths, sanitize control characters, and select a retention and access policy appropriate to the data.

blocks.text: Logging can block or allocate. A high-rate synchronous logger in a reactor can distort the very latency being measured. Use a bounded logging path with an explicit drop or fallback policy and a counter for lost diagnostics. An unbounded asynchronous logger merely moves the memory problem to another queue.

blocks.text: During an incident, increase detail narrowly by operation, component, or time window. Turning on global per-byte logging for every connection can make an overloaded service less recoverable. Preserve the ability to turn diagnostic detail back down.

topics.title: 23.3.2 Using Histograms Without Inventing Precision
topics.summary: A histogram records counts within defined buckets and can support aggregate latency analysis. Its resolution depends on bucket boundaries. A reported percentile derived from coarse buckets is an estimate, not an exact stored request duration.

cards.question: Explain Using Histograms Without Inventing Precision in your own words.
cards.answer: A histogram records counts within defined buckets and can support aggregate latency analysis. Its resolution depends on bucket boundaries. A reported percentile derived from coarse buckets is an estimate, not an exact stored request duration.

blocks.text: 23.3.2 Using Histograms Without Inventing Precision
rich: 23.3.2 Using Histograms Without Inventing Precision

blocks.text: A histogram records counts within defined buckets and can support aggregate latency analysis. Its resolution depends on bucket boundaries. A reported percentile derived from coarse buckets is an estimate, not an exact stored request duration.
rich: A histogram records counts within defined buckets and can support aggregate latency analysis. Its resolution depends on bucket boundaries. A reported percentile derived from coarse buckets is an estimate, not an exact stored request duration.

blocks.text: The example uses cumulative buckets at 0.005, 0.02, 0.1, 1.0, and positive infinity seconds. An observation at 0.05 increments the 0.1, 1.0, and infinity cumulative buckets. The infinity count equals the total observation count. Tests verify these relationships.
rich: The example uses cumulative buckets at 0.005, 0.02, 0.1, 1.0, and positive infinity seconds. An observation at 0.05 increments the 0.1, 1.0, and infinity cumulative buckets. The infinity count equals the total observation count. Tests verify these relationships.

blocks.text: Do not average percentiles from separate instances and call the result a fleet percentile. Aggregate the underlying distribution representation using a supported method, then estimate the percentile. The same caution applies to mixing different bucket definitions or measurement boundaries.
rich: Do not average percentiles from separate instances and call the result a fleet percentile. Aggregate the underlying distribution representation using a supported method, then estimate the percentile. The same caution applies to mixing different bucket definitions or measurement boundaries.

blocks.text: Histograms should observe finite nonnegative durations. A negative value from a wrong clock or a NaN from bad arithmetic should be rejected or categorized, not silently poison aggregate state. The model validates its observations for that reason.

reading.title: 23.3.2 Using Histograms Without Inventing Precision
paragraphs: A histogram records counts within defined buckets and can support aggregate latency analysis. Its resolution depends on bucket boundaries. A reported percentile derived from coarse buckets is an estimate, not an exact stored request duration.

The example uses cumulative buckets at 0.005, 0.02, 0.1, 1.0, and positive infinity seconds. An observation at 0.05 increments the 0.1, 1.0, and infinity cumulative buckets. The infinity count equals the total observation count. Tests verify these relationships.

Do not average percentiles from separate instances and call the result a fleet percentile. Aggregate the underlying distribution representation using a supported method, then estimate the percentile. The same caution applies to mixing different bucket definitions or measurement boundaries.

Histograms should observe finite nonnegative durations. A negative value from a wrong clock or a NaN from bad arithmetic should be rejected or categorized, not silently poison aggregate state. The model validates its observations for that reason.

reading.title: Engineering case — Reconcile attempt counters with durable job state
paragraphs: During a lost-reply test, one logical job produces two dispatcher attempts, one worker receipt, and one gateway completion. A dashboard that counts all worker responses as completed jobs can report two completions. A dashboard that counts only client-observed responses can report zero if the caller stopped waiting before either result was seen.

Neither counter is necessarily wrong; its name and interpretation are wrong if it claims a different boundary. Define dispatch_attempts as transport attempts, worker_receipts as retained logical effects, and jobs_completed as gateway completion transitions. Their expected relationships depend on the recovery protocol.

A restart resets in-memory attempt counters while durable receipts remain. The monitoring system needs to handle that reset and should not subtract the new counter from the old value as if traffic became negative. Exact historical business counts should come from retained authoritative records or a correctly maintained event ledger, not a volatile process metric alone.

Pending count and pending age reveal different problems. Ten recent jobs can be ordinary load; one job pending for a day can indicate a poison operation or lost recovery path. Add an age signal with a defined clock and persistence representation rather than assuming that count alone describes backlog health.

For traces, connect the first attempt’s worker commit, lost reply, second attempt’s receipt lookup, and gateway completion. The first attempt can be unsuccessful from the client’s waiting perspective while the worker effect is successful. A trace viewer should not force those observations into one Boolean.

A useful incident report includes a small reconciliation table: accepted unique keys, completed gateway keys, worker receipt keys, and unresolved differences. Protect the identifiers according to policy, and avoid running an unbounded full-table dump on a busy production system. The lab’s small private databases make direct inspection safe for teaching, but scale changes the diagnostic method.

This case gives observability a correctness role. Signals should help explain the invariant rather than obscure it with attractive aggregate numbers. When the counts disagree, investigate the boundary definitions before assuming the database or monitoring system is broken.
